mcqs.q: Regarding the definition of an EHR:
opts: There is no universally accepted definition
There is one strict global definition
It is defined only by patients
mcqs.explain: There is no universally accepted definition of an EHR; it is also known as EMR, CMR, ECIS and CPR.

mcqs.q: The EHR is best described as the:
opts: Larger system that includes the EMR and PHR and interfaces with many systems
Same thing as a single paper chart
mcqs.explain: The EHR is the larger system that includes the EMR and PHR and interfaces with multiple systems locally, regionally and nationally.

mcqs.q: An EMR (electronic medical record) is a record managed:
opts: By authorized clinicians within ONE healthcare organization
mcqs.explain: An EMR is the electronic patient record created, gathered and consulted by authorized clinicians/staff within one healthcare organization.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes the EHR from the EMR?
opts: The EHR works across MORE THAN ONE organization (interoperable)
The EHR is always on paper
The EHR is only used by patients
mcqs.explain: The EHR conforms to interoperability standards and is used across more than one healthcare organization, whereas the EMR is limited to one.

mcqs.q: The PHR (personal health record) is mainly:
opts: Drawn from multiple sources and controlled by the individual
mcqs.explain: The PHR conforms to interoperability standards and can be drawn from multiple sources while being managed, shared and controlled by the individual.

mcqs.q: The two main TYPES of EHR are:
mcqs.explain: EHRs are classified as outpatient (ambulatory) and inpatient.

mcqs.q: Which is a LIMITATION of paper records?
opts: Illegible handwriting and inability to be shared electronically
mcqs.explain: Paper records have illegible handwriting, cannot be shared/stored electronically, are not structured, are expensive to copy/store, are easily destroyed and slow to retrieve.

mcqs.q: How does an EHR improve EFFICIENCY?
opts: Rapid lab retrieval and reduced duplicate tests/prescriptions
mcqs.explain: EHRs retrieve lab results rapidly, reduce duplicated tests/prescriptions, cut redundant paperwork, interface with billing and avoid phone tag.

mcqs.q: Which is a patient-SAFETY mechanism of the EHR?
opts: Clinical decision support reminding of allergies and correct dosages
mcqs.explain: Safety is improved through legibility, anytime access, reduced duplication, reminders, clinical decision support (allergies, dosing) and problem summary lists.

mcqs.q: An electronic 'problem summary list' provides:
opts: Diagnoses, allergies and surgeries at a glance
mcqs.explain: Electronic problem summary lists provide diagnoses, allergies and surgeries at a glance.

mcqs.q: A FINANCIAL saving from EHR adoption is:
opts: Eliminated chart rooms and reduced transcription costs
mcqs.explain: Financial savings include eliminated chart rooms/clerks, less transcription, fewer pharmacist callbacks, lower copying costs, more patients per day and decreased malpractice.

mcqs.q: A GOVERNMENTAL expectation of EHRs is:
opts: An interoperable EHR and coordinated disease management for older patients
mcqs.explain: Government expectations include an interoperable electronic health record and coordinated disease management in older patients.

mcqs.q: Why do older, more complicated patients particularly benefit from EHRs?
opts: They often have several physicians, so coordination & communication improve
They see only one doctor ever
mcqs.explain: Older patients commonly have more than one physician; EHRs improve coordination of care and communication between disparate healthcare entities.

mcqs.q: Which is a desirable KEY COMPONENT of an EHR?
opts: Clinical decision support, CPOE and secure messaging
mcqs.explain: Desirable components include CDSS, secure messaging, practice-management/portal interfaces, referral management, electronic retrieval of reports, CPOE and the electronic encounter.

mcqs.q: Computerized physician order entry (CPOE) processes orders for:
opts: Medications, lab tests, x-rays, consults and diagnostics
mcqs.explain: CPOE is an EHR feature that processes orders for medications, lab tests, x-rays, consults and other diagnostic tests.

mcqs.q: A benefit of CPOE is that it:
opts: Reduces medication errors, costs and variation of care
mcqs.explain: CPOE reduces medication errors, reduces costs and reduces variation of care.

mcqs.q: A clinical decision support system (CDSS) works by:
opts: Matching a patient's characteristics to a knowledge base to generate recommendations
Making all decisions instead of the doctor
mcqs.explain: A CDSS matches characteristics of individual patients to a computerized knowledge base to generate patient-specific assessments or recommendations for clinicians.

mcqs.q: Most CDSS systems:
opts: Offer alternatives and reminders but make NO decisions on their own
mcqs.explain: Most EHR decision-support systems may offer alternatives and provide reminders but make no decisions on their own.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of an open-source/free EHR?
mcqs.explain: Open-source/free EHRs include OpenVista, WorldVistA and Medsphere OpenVista; comprehensive ones include AHLTA and VA VistA.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognised BARRIER to EHR adoption?
opts: Need for standardized terminology, privacy/security concerns and integration difficulties
mcqs.explain: Historic barriers include the need for standardized clinical terminology, privacy/confidentiality/security concerns, physician data-entry challenges and integration difficulties.

mcqs.q: Which is another (non-historic) barrier to EHR adoption?
opts: Financial cost, physician resistance and loss of productivity
mcqs.explain: Other barriers include financial cost, physician resistance, loss of productivity, workflow changes, lack of standards, adverse legislation and inadequate proof of benefit.

mcqs.q: A technological advance enabling images to be part of the EHR is:
opts: Improved computer speed, memory and digital imaging
mcqs.explain: Computer speed, memory and bandwidth advanced so digital imaging became a reality, letting images be part of an EHR; wireless/mobile tech also enables access.

saqs.q: Differentiate the EHR, EMR and PHR.
saqs.a: EMR = record managed by clinicians within ONE organization. PHR = drawn from multiple sources, managed and controlled by the individual. EHR = the larger, interoperable system used across MORE THAN ONE organization (includes EMR & PHR).

saqs.q: List the limitations of paper records.
saqs.a: Illegible handwriting; cannot be shared/stored electronically; not structured; expensive to copy, transport & store; easily destroyed; difficult to analyze; slow retrieval; can go missing (and an environmental impact).

saqs.q: How do EHRs improve quality of care and patient safety?
saqs.a: Improved legibility, anytime/anywhere access, reduced duplication, reminders for overdue tests, clinical decision support (allergies, dosing) and problem summary lists.

saqs.q: List key components of an EHR.
saqs.a: CDSS, secure messaging, practice-management/scheduling/portal interface, referral management, electronic retrieval of lab/x-ray reports & prior encounters, CPOE, and the electronic patient encounter.

saqs.q: What is CPOE and what are its benefits?
saqs.a: Computerized physician order entry processes orders for medications, labs, x-rays, consults and diagnostics. Benefits: reduces medication errors, costs and variation of care.

Need for standardized terminology, privacy/security concerns, data-entry challenges, integration difficulties, financial cost, physician resistance, lost productivity, workflow change, lack of standards and inadequate proof of benefit.
